title: Corpse or creature
meaning: 'Body' is a dead or dying entity; 'remains' means bones, drops, fragments or loot after death.
pros: Natural wording and Frozen Corpse setting; mob death produces material.
cons: Almost every mob fits. No named creature or recipe is identified.
check: Find a clue selecting one entity and a distinct remaining drop.
assessment: I think it's a sensible literal reading, but too broad for another random drop test.

title: Soul, ghost or surviving effect
meaning: The physical creature disappears, but a soul, spirit, buff or temporary effect remains.
pros: 'Body is not enough' contrasts physical and intangible survival.
cons: Most soul-related items have broad negative tests; no assembly target.
check: Identify one named effect surviving a specific disappearance.
assessment: I would reopen this only if we find an actual survivor and how to combine it.

title: Corpse possessions and recovered loot
meaning: What remains is the dead person's belongings, not their body.
pros: R1's chestplate and journal are found through Frozen Corpse progression.
cons: The dead person's identity and possessions aren't uniquely established.
check: Check primary game lore for a named owner or reconstructable possession.
assessment: I like the direct Hunt connection, but we still need a specific object.

title: Incomplete item body / base
meaning: The body is an item's shell, frame or base and needs components, upgrades or strings.
pros: 'Not enough' naturally implies missing parts; crafting and reforging exist.
cons: No single base item is selected. Many native-assembly tests were negative.
check: Find explicit item lore naming a body, missing parts and a recipe.
assessment: I see this as plausible wording, not a reason to test every craft.

title: Armor torso absent, other pieces remain
meaning: The chestplate is the 'body' armor. The helmet, leggings and boots are what remain of a set.
pros: The Hunt begins with a Dead Man's Chestplate; armor sets have other slots.
cons: No confirmed Dead Man armor set. Other armor pieces have been thrown already.
check: Look for a real set or a clue selecting three specific armor pieces.
assessment: Without a named set, I don't think we should keep guessing armor.

title: Container disappears, contents revealed
meaning: An outer object is removed while something previously hidden inside survives.
pros: This is exactly what happens to the Chestplate and Journal in R1.
cons: R1 is not proof of a general transformation mechanic; no R6 container identified.
check: Find another explicit 'inside' or concealed-item source and a checkable action.
assessment: This is the cleanest proven model of disappearance and survival so far.

title: Destroyed item leaves salvage or essence
meaning: Gone means broken/consumed; remains means usable scrap, essence or residue.
pros: Salvaging and dismantling are real game processes.
cons: Direct Chestplate salvage refused; no chosen salvage chain.
check: Identify a specific destruction output that itself has an assembly recipe.
assessment: I don't want to repeat salvage without an item-specific reason.

title: Body of text
meaning: Body means the contents of the Journal or another written text; remains are selected letters or words.
pros: R1 uses a real acrostic, so text extraction has precedent.
cons: No reproducible extraction rule yields a credible R6 operation.
check: Require one deterministic rule, applied consistently to the known lines.
assessment: I think this deserves space in the hub, separate from music.

title: Body of water
meaning: Body means the Great Glacite Lake or another water body; absence implies freeze, drainage or a vanished object within it.
pros: The lake is central to every confirmed offering.
cons: The lake has not been observed disappearing, and almost any ice clue fits.
check: Identify a real change to a named water body and a surviving item.
assessment: The location connection is obvious but the proposed disappearance isn't.

title: Collective body or group
meaning: Body means a group, cult or team, and 'assemble' means gather members.
pros: Better Together, Cult and multi-player mechanics exist.
cons: No specific group or number is selected by R6 wording.
check: Look for NPC dialogue directly describing a dissolved group or surviving members.
assessment: I prefer this as a group-mechanic branch rather than a generic four-player test.

title: Main part versus supporting components
meaning: Body may mean the main portion of a device or organism, while smaller non-body pieces survive.
pros: Some native items have a frame, pegs, strings, plates or replaceable modules.
cons: No named device, component list or causal 'gone' event.
check: Find a preexisting base-and-pieces mechanic that uses the wording.
assessment: This is broader than the harp analogy and should appear before it.

title: Pieces, fragments or drops
meaning: 'Remains' denotes tangible leftovers that must become one constructed item.
pros: Fossil, shard and fragment reconstruction all exist.
cons: This expands into too many candidates with no selector.
check: Require a known fragment set and native result.
assessment: I think assembly needs an actual resulting object to be persuasive.

title: Information, memory or recorded name
meaning: When physical offerings vanish, their names, sequence or Journal entries remain.
pros: The Journal records riddle progress and the R1 acrostic is established.
cons: The puzzle text doesn't supply a unique operation or letter rule.
check: Test a consistent rule on known answers with an independently meaningful output.
assessment: I don't want to confuse a neat word pattern with a verified decoder.

title: Craft or forge the survivor
meaning: Assemble means actual crafting, forging, fusion or combination, possibly inside the lake.
pros: The imperative 'assemble' sounds actionable; SkyBlock has native recipes.
cons: The Hunt hasn't shown it detects arbitrary crafting; several attempts already happened.
check: Find a selected recipe and separate crafting from item-offering tests.
assessment: A concrete recipe would matter much more than the word 'craft' alone.

title: Arrange or co-locate several entities
meaning: Assemble means place items together in the lake, not use a crafting grid.
pros: R5 succeeds when three Calling units are present before Feather arrival.
cons: R5 does not prove R6 works the same way or uses a set size.
check: Find a specific set and test arrival order versus simultaneous presence.
assessment: This has a real earlier-step precedent, but needs an identified set.

title: Gather players in one area
meaning: Assemble means bringing people together, perhaps at event end.
pros: Better Together is a real same-zone multiplayer event.
cons: No evidence that the hunt uses player count or event timing.
check: Record exact player count, same-zone state and Journal before/after.
assessment: Without a selected trigger, I'd avoid asking for a large group.

title: Absence after an item despawns
meaning: The requirement happens only once an item is no longer present.
pros: R4 checks arrival and R5 checks presence; a change of state is plausible.
cons: Pickup, despawn and server consumption differ; older tests wait in different ways.
check: Compare a precise disappearance event against a controlled remaining item.
assessment: This is still worth a controlled test, but only with a named item.

title: Quest consumption rather than natural expiry
meaning: 'Gone' refers to a successfully consumed puzzle offering, not ordinary disappearance.
pros: R1 and R5 show offerings consumed by the lake as the Journal advances.
cons: No proof R6 builds on earlier consumed offerings or checks history.
check: Look for a reproducible Journal-state or consumption-dependent reaction.
assessment: I think this distinction is important for interpreting old failed tests.

title: Two clauses, possibly separate tasks
meaning: 'The body is not enough' specifies a condition; 'assemble ...' specifies another action.
pros: The clue has two sentences with different grammatical roles.
cons: Most natural 'it' still refers to body, and two steps aren't established.
check: A candidate must explain both requirements without extra assumptions.
assessment: I want to keep this grammatical reading open rather than force one story.

title: 'It' refers to something else
meaning: The pronoun may refer to a different object, event or group instead of 'the body'.
pros: Riddle language sometimes hides the relevant object.
cons: English grammar more naturally links 'it' to body; search space grows quickly.
check: Find a second named referent from an earlier clue or game dialogue.
assessment: This is possible but too unconstrained until another source narrows it.

title: Echo: voice remains after body disappears
meaning: Ovid's Echo loses her body, retaining a voice and bones that turn into stone; repetition could suggest a word mechanic.
pros: The body/voice/remains language closely resembles the clue.
cons: No in-game target or physical assembly. Voice and bones do not assemble in the poem.
check: Look for an independently selected Echo-type action, not arbitrary chat spam.
assessment: The wording is strong, but I still can't map 'assemble' to gameplay.

title: Orpheus: lyre and voice surviving death
meaning: In Ovid XI, Orpheus's head and lyre float to the sea while sound persists.
pros: Music, water and survival overlap with several Hunt discussions.
cons: The myth doesn't establish DEFAG as Orpheus's notes or a game recipe.
check: Verify source quotations and distinguish myth from item/music tests.
assessment: I don't think the lyre alone selects a R6 item.

title: Kalevala's fish-bone kantele and lost harp
meaning: A pike-bone instrument is assembled from remains; later a lost kantele is replaced by a birch one.
pros: Explicit crafting from remains and lost-in-water story.
cons: It is not a documented Hunt reference; no selected SkyBlock process.
check: Find game lore tying Melody's harp reconstruction to lake mechanics.
assessment: I enjoy the parallel, but I won't elevate it above literal readings.

title: Five initials as D E F A G
meaning: First letters of known answer items are musical notes.
pros: All five initials genuinely belong to the natural-note alphabet.
cons: Five matches do not prove a tune or a correct future answer.
check: Judge whether R6 and R7 initials complete B/C as predicted.
assessment: It's a falsifiable prediction, not proof of a melody.

title: Better Together supplies B / play DEFAGB
meaning: Better Together starts with B and has 14 letters without spaces. Proposed performance uses DEFAGB during or after event.
pros: The event's end text refers to an enduring cooperative spirit.
cons: The note sequence and event timing are not implied by a verified clue; DEFAG active-event tests are partial.
check: Only consider a controlled DEFAGB/event-end test with a fixed item/action and Journal check.
assessment: I would not call the earlier mixed music test a full negative here.

title: Seven known answers eventually give seven notes
meaning: The first seven answers might cover C D E F G A B once each, rather than requiring a performance now.
pros: The Journal has 14 slots in 2 rows of 7, and first five initials are distinct note names.
cons: Seven-column UI could be ordinary layout; R6/R7 are unknown.
check: Compare initials after genuinely verified R6 and R7 solves.
assessment: This prediction needs no extra coins and might be wrong later.

title: Visible shadow versus actual light level
meaning: A reported lake silhouette could point to a vanished body or location; separately, a precise real light-level state or transition might be an R6 condition.
pros: Community shadow observation and darker footage are suggestive visuals; Crystal Armor genuinely changes with light levels 0–15.
cons: Night Vision changes visual brightness, not the block-light value; screenshots alone do not verify a special shadow or Hunt mechanic.
check: First locate the original image and reproduce a consistent shadow, then compare actual in-game light data or Crystal Armor response at fixed lake positions while controlling client lighting settings and Journal state.
evidence_type: Reported visual / confirmed ordinary light mechanic
assessment: I want to distinguish a graphic effect from a reproducible light-level state before requesting another item test.

title: Assemble the survivor, not the insufficient body
meaning: The clause 'the body is not enough' is purpose-relative: not enough TO FIND OUT WHAT COMES NEXT. A body could be complete and useful for its normal function yet fail as a source of the next clue. The riddle does not request repairing or rebuilding it. 'Assemble that which remains when it is gone' may require a new product, a useful subset, information, or other survivors after the body disappears. This includes (unverified) filtering away irrelevant parts, but the wording does not require such filtering.
pros: Grammar: 'not enough' is restricted by the explicit goal 'to find out which comes next', not a universal defect in the body. The imperative targets 'that which remains', not reconstruction of the body. 'Remains' means whatever continues to exist, not necessarily body fragments. R1 shows a different object (Journal) appearing when Chestplate vanishes, but the Journal was intact.
cons: No chosen body, normal purpose, missing informational function, survivor set, filtering rule, or native assembly action. The clause can also be read as 'body plus other necessary things', rather than exclusion of bodily material. Rebuilding the body could theoretically still be one intermediate step, so it cannot be ruled out by grammar alone.
check: For a candidate, specify (1) its normal function, (2) the exact task it is insufficient for, (3) what disappearance does: produce, expose, or merely time the next action, (4) what survives independently, (5) a source-selected assembly, and (6) expected R6 Journal feedback. Reject candidate if the interpretation needs unselected deletions or invented effects. See I029.
evidence_type: New grammatical interpretation; no R6 test
assessment: Most useful constraint: 'not enough' means insufficient for finding the next step, not incomplete overall. I should not assume repairing the body or returning to it is the goal, nor assume parts are removed because they are bad. Next we need evidence of what disappears and what different result is assembled.

title: Gone as production, revelation or timing
meaning: The phrase 'when it is gone' has several possible jobs. Production: disappearance creates fragments. Revelation: removal exposes survivors already present. Timing/state: the body is absent and independent objects or information are available for assembly. Importantly 'when it is gone' need not tell the player to cause or witness disappearance: the body might have been gone before the Hunt began, and the task is to assemble existing traces left behind. The body can be complete for its normal function but insufficient for finding the next clue.
pros: R1 proves revelation in the Hunt: the Chestplate is consumed and an intact Journal hidden inside emerges. R5 proves pre-existing items can serve as a state condition. The clue says 'when it is gone', not 'destroy the body' or 'wait for it to disappear'; a past absence is grammatically compatible, though not established as intended.
cons: No source yet identifies the body, dates its disappearance, or names an assembly target. A past disappearance, newly created fragments, revealed survivors and after-event conditions are all live alternatives; grammar alone cannot select between them.
check: For each source-selected candidate, ask whether the body is already absent before the player acts, or whether its disappearance must be caused. If a fresh event exists, distinguish newly produced drops, revealed existing objects, and a condition change. If the disappearance was historical, identify independently documented survivor objects and a fixed assembly action. Require R6-stage Journal evidence. No random throws.
evidence_type: Grammar-derived causal alternatives; no R6 validation
assessment: Do not assume we have to kill/destroy/vanish anything in the present. An already-gone dead man and surviving records are a coherent literary reading, not yet evidence of the game solution. Seek a specific surviving set and why it reveals the next step.
